what: TeraWulf operates data centres. It began by mining bitcoin using cheap, largely carbon-free power in New York and Pennsylvania, and is now converting that power and land into hosting facilities for artificial intelligence computing, leased to companies that need large amounts of electricity for their own hardware.
customers: Originally itself, as a bitcoin miner. Increasingly, large technology and AI companies that lease data centre capacity under long contracts because they cannot secure grid connections fast enough themselves.
money: Mining revenue from its own bitcoin production.
Long-term leases of power and data centre capacity to AI and high-performance computing customers.
moat: The scarce asset is not computers but electricity: an existing grid connection with hundreds of megawatts available takes years and sometimes a decade to obtain, and in many regions it simply cannot be had. TeraWulf secured that capacity for mining when nobody wanted it, and it is now the binding constraint for AI computing.
risks: A trailing net loss of $784.2M and free cash flow of about negative $3.1B — the business is consuming enormous amounts of capital to build facilities.
Debt of $3.1B against $3.3B of cash funds the construction, and the financing has been raised repeatedly through both borrowing and share issuance, which dilutes existing holders.
Revenue of $190.8M against a $5.8B market value is 30.4 times sales, so essentially all of the value is in contracts not yet earning.
Bitcoin mining economics are poor and getting worse, so the old business cannot support the company if the new one is delayed.
Twenty-four analysts average a $25.52 target against an $11.59 price, a 120% gap that signals a share price driven by sentiment rather than earnings.
opportunities: Revenue has grown from $13.4M in 2020 to $168.5M in 2025, and the hosting contracts signed point considerably higher.
Secured power capacity with grid interconnection is the genuine bottleneck in AI infrastructure, and TeraWulf holds it.
Long-term leases with creditworthy technology customers convert a volatile commodity business into contracted revenue.
Cash of $3.3B gives the company the resources to complete the build-out it has committed to.
watch: Contracted capacity in megawatts and the credit quality of the counterparties. Nothing on the income statement describes this company yet; the signed leases do.
view: TeraWulf is not really a bitcoin company any more, and anyone analysing it as one will reach the wrong answer. What it owns is electricity — secured grid interconnections with hundreds of megawatts available, in places where that capacity exists. It acquired that asset when the only use anyone could think of was mining bitcoin, which was a cheap way to monetise power nobody else wanted. Then AI arrived and made large blocks of available power the single scarcest input in computing.

That is a genuinely fortunate position and it is worth being clear about why it is durable. New grid connections of this size take years and in many regions cannot be obtained at all: transmission capacity is limited, utilities are oversubscribed, and local opposition is real. A technology company with unlimited money still cannot buy a 300-megawatt interconnection that does not exist. It can only rent one from somebody who already has it. That is the business TeraWulf is converting into.

The financial picture is correspondingly brutal and should not be smoothed over. Free cash flow of roughly negative $3.1 billion, a net loss of $784 million, $3.1 billion of debt, and repeated equity issuance that dilutes anyone who bought earlier. This is a construction company at the moment, and the revenue of $191 million bears no relationship to the $5.8 billion market value. The entire valuation rests on contracts that have been signed but not yet earned.

So the honest framing is binary rather than analytical. If the facilities get built on schedule and the counterparties pay, contracted revenue arrives and the valuation makes sense. If construction slips, financing tightens, or an AI customer reconsiders its capacity commitments, the mining business underneath cannot support $3.1 billion of debt — bitcoin economics are poor and deteriorating. The twenty-four analysts at $25.52 against an $11.59 price are not forecasting; they are expressing how wide the range of outcomes is. Watch contracted megawatts and who signed for them, and treat everything else here as noise.
bull: Contracted AI hosting capacity comes online on schedule with creditworthy counterparties, turning scarce secured power into years of contracted revenue.
bear: Construction slips or a customer pulls back, financing tightens against $3.1 billion of debt, and a failing bitcoin business cannot carry it.
